cards.front: What should you know about reproduction and hormones?
cards.back: The menstrual cycle is controlled by four main hormones. These hormones can be used in contraception and in fertility treatments such as IVF.

cards.front: What should you know about the menstrual cycle?
cards.back: is a roughly 28-day cycle in which an egg is released from an ovary and the uterus lining is prepared for a possible pregnancy. If the egg is not fertilised, the uterus lining breaks down (menstruation/period).

cards.front: What should you know about hormone interactions?
cards.back: FSH stimulates oestrogen production Oestrogen inhibits FSH (negative feedback) and stimulates LH LH triggers ovulation Progesterone inhibits both FSH and LH If progesterone levels fall (no pregnancy), the uterus lining breaks down and the cycle restarts

cards.front: What should you know about contraception?
cards.back: prevents pregnancy by preventing ovulation, preventing fertilisation, or preventing implantation of a fertilised egg.

cards.front: What should you know about ivf?
cards.back: is a fertility treatment used when a woman cannot conceive naturally. It involves stimulating the ovaries to produce multiple eggs, collecting them, fertilising them in a laboratory, and implanting embryos into the uterus.

cards.front: What should you know about ivf process?
cards.back: Give the woman FSH and LH to stimulate the ovaries to produce multiple mature eggs (superovulation) Collect the eggs from the ovaries Fertilise the eggs with sperm in a laboratory (in vitro = "in glass") Allow the fertilised eggs to develop into embryos Implant 1-2 embryos into the woman's uterus If successful, the embryo implants in the uterus lining and pregnancy begins

cards.front: What should you know about ethical issues with ivf?
cards.back: IVF is expensive and not always available on the NHS — access may be limited Multiple embryos are often created but not all are implanted — some may be destroyed, raising ethical concerns about the right to life Multiple births (twins/triplets) are more likely with IVF, which carry higher health risks for mother and babies IVF success rates are not 100% — the emotional and physical stress of failed cycles can be significant Some religious groups object to IVF because it involves fertilisation outside the body and the potential destruction of embryos
Pituitary gland (e.g. Causes an egg to mature in the ovary (inside a follicle). Stimulates the ovaries to produce oestrogen.)
Pituitary gland (e.g. Triggers ovulation (release of the mature egg from the ovary). Stimulates the remains of the follicle to develop into a corpus luteum.)
Ovaries (e.g. Builds up and maintains the uterus lining. Inhibits further FSH production (negative feedback). Stimulates LH release.)
Ovary (corpus luteum) (e.g. Maintains the uterus lining during pregnancy. Inhibits both FSH and LH release (prevents another egg from being released).)

cards.front: What does Combined pill (oral contraceptive) mean?
cards.back: Contains oestrogen and progesterone. Inhibits FSH production so no egg matures. (e.g. Over 99% effective if taken correctly. Can reduce period pain.)

cards.front: What does Progesterone-only pill / injection / implant mean?
cards.back: Progesterone inhibits FSH and LH (prevents ovulation). Also thickens cervical mucus to block sperm. (e.g. Effective. Long-acting options (injection lasts 3 months, implant lasts 3 years).)
Prevents sperm from reaching the egg. Physical barrier. (e.g. Protects against STIs. No side effects from hormones. Easily available.)
Prevents implantation of a fertilised egg. Hormonal IUDs also release progesterone. (e.g. Long-lasting (5-10 years). Very effective.)
